hook.text: Falling water has powered mills for centuries. Now it generates 16% of the world's electricity.

buildup.text: A dam holds back a reservoir. Water flows through turbines at the base, spinning generators.

discovery.text: Hydro is reliable and produces almost no emissions once the dam is built.

twist.text: But dams flood valleys, displace communities, and block fish migration routes.

climax.text: Rotting vegetation in reservoirs can also release methane, especially in the tropics.

punchline.text: Clean power with a complicated price tag.

quiz.question: What share of global electricity comes from hydroelectric power?

details.summary: Hydroelectric power generates electricity by channeling flowing or falling water through turbines. It is the world's largest source of renewable electricity, providing about 16 percent of global supply.
details.whyItMatters: Hydropower provides reliable, dispatchable clean energy and supports grid stability. However, large dams also carry significant social and environmental costs that must be weighed.
takeaways: Hydropower supplies about 16 percent of global electricity
Dam reservoirs allow on-demand power generation
It is the largest source of renewable electricity worldwide

faq.question: What are the environmental downsides of large dams?
faq.answer: Large dams flood valleys, displace communities, block fish migration, alter downstream sediment flow, and can emit methane from decomposing vegetation in reservoirs. These impacts make new large-dam projects increasingly controversial.

faq.question: Which countries produce the most hydroelectric power?
faq.answer: China leads by far, followed by Brazil, Canada, the United States, and Russia. Norway and Paraguay generate nearly all their electricity from hydropower. Global hydroelectric capacity continues to grow, mainly in Asia and Africa.
